If anything below is still ambiguous, I propose a 30-minute technical sync with our SREs (Marcus) and Solutions (Karthik).

Summary answers (short):
- Measurement source: For Redwood Hosted (default) we measure at Redwood egress (edge nodes that terminate customer requests). For Redwood Private we provide the same measurement methodology but will run the measurement logic in-customer (collector deployed as a sidecar) and produce signed reports.

- Uptime window: We use calendar-month for billing and a 30-day rolling window for operational alerts. Service credit eligibility is evaluated on the invoice month. Synthetic checks are included only for service health dashboards; the uptime metric used for credits counts customer-facing request success (see "denominator" below).

- Latency (p50/p95/p99): p99 is computed over successful, non-throttled requests that return a 2xx application response (not including client-side timeouts or 429/5xx). Cold-starts are excluded from the p99 bucket if they are deterministic (e.g., container spin-up when model is scaled down); we annotate and publish the cold-start rate separately.

- Service credit formula: Monthly credit = max_credit * max(0, (SLA_target - Observed_uptime) / SLA_target). Example in the attached appendix (Redwood_SLA_Methodology_Appendix.pdf). Maximum monthly credit cap is 50% of the monthly invoice for the affected service.

- Dispute & telemetry: We accept customer telemetry as a supplement. A dispute must be raised within 30 days of invoice publication; both parties provide logs/queries and we run a joint investigation (typically 7 business days) before credits are issued or contested.

John / Laura —

Following up with more technical precision to address John's questions. Quoting John's ask for clarity:

> "define 'successful, non-throttled requests' exactly in terms of HTTP status classes and internal application-level error codes"

Clarification (tech):
- Success: HTTP 2xx where the application layer returns an inference payload (not an error wrapper). 202 Accepted with async token is treated as success only if we later return a 2xx within the request lifecycle window; otherwise it's treated as incomplete and excluded from p99.
- Excluded: 4xx client errors (except specific client-side validation where we still return a payload), 429 (rate limit) and all 5xx are excluded from p99 calculation but are included in uptime availability calculations as failures. We tag and surface 429 separately in the report.
- Cold-starts: Defined as the first token-generation request served from a newly provisioned instance where the process-level startup time contributes >15% of total wall-time. We instrument and label these; we compute p99 both including and excluding cold-starts and publish both numbers in the monthly report.
- Private / air-gapped deployments: The collector can operate fully air-gapped and produce signed, time-stamped artifacts (HMAC-signed CSVs). Outbound verification is optional but recommended for automated reconciliation.
- Worked example for credits (short): SLA target = 99.9% for the month, Observed uptime = 99.6% => Delta = 0.3% => Apply formula Monthly credit = max_credit * (0.003 / 0.999) ≈ 0.003003 * max_credit. If max_credit = 50% of monthly invoice of $100,000 => max_credit $50,000 => credit ≈ $150.15. (See appendix for table-based examples.)

I attached a machine-friendly SLA_Report_Template.csv that includes columns we typically provide: day, total_requests, successful_requests, p50, p95, p99_including_coldstart, p99_excluding_coldstart, coldstart_count, 5xx_count, 429_count, uptime_pct.

Happy to walk through the template on the sync — Marcus.
